---
title: "Insight from Psychedelic Research"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-31"
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

Research into the antidepressant effects of ketamine and subsequent psychedelics has revolutionized the field. Not only has it introduced the concept of "rapid-acting antidepressants," it has also provided valuable insights into understanding existing therapeutic modalities. Substances like psilocybin, Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and Dimethyltryptamine (DMT) transiently disrupt canonical functional networks and facilitate global re-integration [@Tagliazucchi2018]. This desynchronized state has been dubbed the "entropic brain state," where the brain enters a regime near "criticality" in the attractor landscape [@CarhartHarris2014; @CarhartHarris2019]. It is considered therapeutic, however, as it enables the brain to escape from pathological "stuck loops." Recent fMRI studies have confirmed that this acute desynchronization allows the system to access a broader repertoire of potential brain states [@Siegel2024].

Another important insight is that these substances can reopen critical periods for neuroplastic learning [@Hensch2004; @Patton2019]. A critical period is an early developmental window during which the nervous system is exceptionally sensitive to environmental stimuli. Animal studies have demonstrated that the administration of psychedelics to adult mice can re-engage critical periods, particularly in the context of social reward learning [@Nardou2023]. Re-entering a critical period signifies a substantial elevation in neuroplastic potential, facilitating rapid and sustained modifications in structural and functional connectivity. Reflecting this capacity, psychedelics are often termed "psychoplastogens" [@Vargas2021;@olson2018].

Clinicians practicing psychedelic-assisted psychotherapy view this period as a "window of opportunity" for therapeutic change, emphasizing that structured psychotherapeutic interventions must be provided during this time [@CarhartHarris2018; @Lepow2021; @Lepow2023; @Caulfield2025]. This clinical expertise underscores that the critical period reopened by psychedelics serves as a prime opportunity for fundamental change in any direction.

These features of psychedelics map naturally onto an attractor model of psychopathology. Acute $5\text{-HT}_{2\text{A}}$-mediated perturbation transiently reduces within- and between-network integrity, leading to a temporary “flattening” of the attractor landscape and enhanced metastability [@Roseman2014; @Madsen2021; @Singleton2022]. Following this disruption, a time-limited window of heightened neuroplasticity opens, during which activity-dependent synaptic remodeling is facilitated via BDNF–TrkB-linked pathways. Clinically, the benefit of psychedelics appears to be time-limited; without structured psychotherapy, clinical gains may attenuate as the system relaxes back toward pre-existing maladaptive attractors [@CarhartHarris2018a; @Goodwin2022]. The existence of a time constraint implies that this flattened and malleable state cannot persist indefinitely; it will eventually remodel into a new configuration of valleys and ridges. This emphasizes the importance of the rewiring and homeostasis phases of DPRH model.
